The Case for Legalizing Insider Trading: Efficiency, Liberty, and Rational Markets

A Persuasive Essay

Introduction

Few propositions in financial regulation provoke as visceral a reaction as the suggestion that insider trading should be fully legalized. The very phrase conjures images of cigar-smoking executives enriching themselves at the expense of ordinary investors—a caricature that has calcified into unquestioned orthodoxy since the Securities and Exchange Commission first began prosecuting insider trading cases in earnest during the 1960s. Yet beneath the moral panic lies a serious, rigorous, and deeply compelling body of scholarship arguing that prohibitions on insider trading are not merely unnecessary but actively harmful to the functioning of capital markets, to corporate governance, and to the principles of a free society.

The central thesis of this essay is straightforward: allowing insider trading enhances market efficiency by speeding up the incorporation of private information into stock prices, and the cascade of benefits flowing from this improved efficiency—more accurate capital allocation, stronger corporate governance incentives, reduced systemic risk, and greater respect for property rights—vastly outweighs the speculative harms attributed to the practice. The prohibition of insider trading is a relic of economic misunderstanding, populist sentiment, and regulatory overreach. It is time for a serious reexamination.

I. The Market Efficiency Argument: Information Belongs in Prices

The Foundational Logic

The most powerful argument for legalizing insider trading rests on the efficient market hypothesis and, more broadly, on the universally acknowledged principle that securities markets function best when prices accurately reflect all available information about the underlying value of assets. Accurate prices are not an abstract academic nicety; they are the mechanism by which a market economy allocates capital. When stock prices are wrong—when they fail to reflect material realities about a firm's prospects—capital flows to the wrong places. Factories are built that should not be built, companies are funded that should not be funded, and workers pursue careers in industries destined for failure.

Private information—knowledge held by corporate insiders about impending earnings surprises, product breakthroughs, mergers, regulatory decisions, or operational failures—represents, by definition, information that has not yet been incorporated into market prices. Every moment that this information remains locked inside the minds of executives while stock prices languish at stale valuations is a moment of market inefficiency. The prohibition of insider trading does not prevent the information from existing; it merely prevents it from reaching prices through one of the fastest channels available.

When an insider trades on material nonpublic information, that trade exerts price pressure. If a CEO knows that next quarter's earnings will massively exceed expectations, her purchases of company stock push the price upward—toward the price that will eventually prevail once the information becomes public. The adjustment is incremental but immediate. Other sophisticated market participants, observing unusual volume and price movements, begin their own analysis, accelerating the process further. By the time the formal announcement arrives, the price shock is dampened, volatility is reduced, and the market has already done much of its adjustive work.

The Scholarship of Henry Manne

This argument was first systematically articulated by Henry Manne in his landmark 1966 book Insider Trading and the Stock Market. Manne demonstrated that insider trading serves as a decentralized, low-cost mechanism for communicating information that would otherwise remain impounded until a formal disclosure event. His argument was not merely theoretical; it was grounded in the observable reality that prices adjust continuously as traders act on heterogeneous information. Insider trading, Manne argued, is simply one form of informed trading—and all informed trading makes markets more efficient.

In the decades since Manne's work, a substantial body of empirical research has supported his thesis. Studies have consistently found that markets in which insiders trade more freely exhibit faster price discovery. Conversely, stricter enforcement of insider trading laws has been associated with slower adjustment of prices to new information, greater price volatility around earnings announcements, and wider bid-ask spreads—all hallmarks of reduced efficiency.

The Comparative Institutional Analysis

It is essential to ask: if not insider trading, then what mechanism will ensure that private information reaches prices? The current regime relies primarily on mandatory disclosure rules—periodic filings, Regulation FD, and the like. But mandatory disclosure is inherently slow, incomplete, and subject to gaming. Companies disclose on schedules dictated by regulation, not by the urgency of the information. Between disclosure events, prices drift in ignorance. Analyst research partially fills the gap, but analysts face their own conflicts of interest, lack the granular knowledge that insiders possess, and are prone to herding behavior.

Insider trading, by contrast, operates continuously, requires no bureaucratic apparatus, and is driven by the strongest possible incentive: the profit motive of those with the most accurate information. It is, in essence, a private-sector alternative to regulatory disclosure—faster, cheaper, and more responsive to the actual flow of material developments within firms.

II. Debunking the "Unfairness" Objection

The Myth of a Level Playing Field

The most common objection to insider trading is that it is "unfair" to ordinary investors who lack access to inside information. This objection, while emotionally resonant, collapses under scrutiny. The securities markets have never been, are not, and cannot be a level playing field. Institutional investors employ armies of analysts, deploy sophisticated quantitative models, maintain privileged relationships with corporate management (within the boundaries of Regulation FD, but only barely), and enjoy technological advantages—including co-located servers for high-frequency trading—that dwarf any informational edge possessed by a corporate insider buying a few thousand shares.

The fiction of informational equality is precisely that: a fiction. The retail investor who purchases shares of a company has always traded at a disadvantage relative to better-informed market participants. What matters is not whether all traders possess identical information—an impossible condition—but whether the prices at which transactions occur are reasonably accurate reflections of fundamental value. If insider trading improves price accuracy, then the retail investor is better off in a world with insider trading, not worse, because the price she pays more closely approximates the true value of what she is buying.

The Anonymous Market Counterparty Problem

Critics frequently invoke the image of an insider "taking advantage" of an unsuspecting counterparty. But in modern electronic securities markets, trades are executed anonymously through centralized exchanges. The person selling shares to an insider is not a specific, identifiable victim; she is someone who had already independently decided to sell at the prevailing market price. She would have sold regardless of whether the insider was the buyer. If anything, the insider's purchases cause the price to be slightly higher than it otherwise would have been, meaning the seller receives a better price because of the insider's participation.

The alleged victim of insider trading is largely a phantom—a construction of regulatory rhetoric rather than a flesh-and-blood individual who has suffered a cognizable harm.

III. Corporate Governance and Compensation Benefits

Insider Trading as an Efficient Compensation Mechanism

Manne's second major insight was that insider trading can serve as an efficient form of entrepreneurial compensation. In any corporation, value is created by individuals who generate innovations, identify opportunities, or make decisions that cannot be fully specified in advance by employment contracts. The problem of compensating such entrepreneurial contributions is one of the oldest puzzles in organizational economics. Stock options and restricted stock grants are partial solutions, but they are blunt instruments—awarded on schedules, subject to vesting periods, and frequently decoupled from specific value-creating actions.

Insider trading, by contrast, allows the individual who generates a valuable innovation or makes a crucial strategic decision to capture a portion of the value she has created, precisely at the moment of creation, in proportion to the magnitude of her contribution. It is a self-executing, self-calibrating compensation mechanism that requires no committee deliberation, no proxy statement disclosure, and no shareholder vote. By aligning the interests of value creators with the immediate market consequences of their actions, insider trading provides sharper incentives for entrepreneurial risk-taking than any formal compensation plan.

Disciplining Poor Management

The benefits run in both directions. Just as insiders who generate positive information can profit from purchases, insiders who observe deteriorating conditions and sell their holdings send a powerful signal to the market. In a world where insider trading is legal, a wave of insider selling would rapidly depress a company's stock price, alerting outside investors, creditors, and board members to potential problems far earlier than the current system of delayed disclosures permits. This accelerated feedback loop disciplines poor management and reduces the duration of value-destroying strategies.

IV. The Costs of Prohibition

Regulatory Overreach and the Erosion of Legal Clarity

The prohibition of insider trading in the United States is notoriously ill-defined. Unlike most criminal offenses, insider trading has never been comprehensively defined by statute. The SEC and the courts have constructed the offense through a patchwork of judicial opinions—Chiarella, Dirks, O'Hagan, Newman, Martoma—that have produced a body of law so convoluted that even experienced securities attorneys cannot reliably predict what conduct will be deemed illegal. The "classical theory," the "misappropriation theory," and the ever-shifting definition of "personal benefit" create traps for the unwary and windfalls for the well-counseled.

This legal uncertainty is itself a cost. It chills legitimate information-gathering and trading activity, discourages corporate insiders from making trades that would improve price discovery, and diverts prosecutorial resources toward cases that often rest on ambiguous facts and contestable legal theories. The enormous expense of insider trading investigations—wiretaps, forensic data analysis, years-long grand jury proceedings—consumes resources that could be directed toward genuinely harmful forms of financial fraud.

Enforcement Futility

Despite decades of aggressive enforcement, there is little evidence that insider trading has been substantially deterred. The SEC brings a few dozen cases per year out of millions of trades. Academic studies consistently find abnormal returns associated with legal insider transactions reported on Form 4, suggesting that insiders routinely trade profitably on the basis of superior information—information that may not meet the legal threshold of "material nonpublic information" but is economically indistinguishable from it. The line between legal informed trading and illegal insider trading is, in practice, a line drawn in water.

If the prohibition cannot be effectively enforced, and if the attempt to enforce it generates enormous costs in legal uncertainty, regulatory expenditure, and chilled legitimate activity, then the case for maintaining the prohibition must rest on benefits substantial enough to justify these costs. As argued above, those benefits are largely illusory.

V. Philosophical and Constitutional Considerations

Property Rights in Information

A final set of arguments concerns the fundamental question of who owns information. In a free society, information generated within a corporation can plausibly be regarded as the property of the corporation or of the individuals who generated it. If it is the corporation's property, then the corporation should be free to authorize or prohibit insider trading by its employees as a matter of private contract—not government regulation. Some companies might choose to prohibit insider trading to maintain investor confidence; others might permit it as a form of compensation. This contractual approach, advocated by scholars across the ideological spectrum, respects firm autonomy and allows experimentation.

If insider trading regulation were replaced by private contractual arrangements, the resulting diversity of corporate policies would generate valuable information about which approach shareholders actually prefer—a market test that the current one-size-fits-all prohibition prevents.

Freedom of Contract and Economic Liberty

The prohibition of insider trading is, at its core, a restriction on the freedom of individuals to enter into voluntary transactions on the basis of their own knowledge and judgment. In a liberal society, the burden of justification falls on those who would restrict freedom, not on those who would exercise it. For the reasons elaborated throughout this essay, the proponents of prohibition have failed to meet that burden. The harms attributed to insider trading are speculative and often illusory; the benefits of legalization are grounded in well-established economic theory and supported by empirical evidence.

VI. Addressing Remaining Counterarguments

"Investor Confidence Will Collapse"

The most frequently invoked policy argument is that legalized insider trading would undermine investor confidence and drive retail investors from the market. But this prediction is undermined by history and comparative evidence. Before the SEC began aggressively prosecuting insider trading in the 1960s, the American securities markets were already the deepest and most liquid in the world—despite the widespread understanding that insiders traded on private information. Many countries with less stringent insider trading enforcement have thriving capital markets. Hong Kong, for example, did not criminalize insider trading until 2003, yet its stock exchange was among the world's largest and most active long before that date.

Moreover, the "investor confidence" argument proves too much. If the goal is to maximize retail investor participation, one could equally argue for prohibiting high-frequency trading, restricting short selling, or banning institutional investors from trading altogether—interventions that few would endorse. Confidence should be grounded in price accuracy, not in the illusion that all traders are equally informed.

"Insiders Will Delay or Manipulate Disclosures"

A more sophisticated objection holds that legalizing insider trading would incentivize insiders to delay corporate disclosures in order to trade profitably on private information. This concern is legitimate but overstated. Existing fiduciary duties and securities disclosure requirements would continue to govern the timing of corporate announcements. An executive who deliberately delays a material disclosure to profit from trading would still be in breach of her fiduciary obligations—a violation actionable under state corporate law and federal securities law independent of any insider trading prohibition.

Furthermore, in a world of legal insider trading, the observable behavior of insiders—purchases, sales, volume patterns—would itself become a rich source of information for outside investors, analysts, and the financial press. Any delay in formal disclosure would be partially offset by the accelerated price discovery that insider trading provides.

Conclusion

The case for fully legalizing insider trading is not a case for lawlessness, deception, or the exploitation of ordinary investors. It is a case for allowing the price system to function as it was designed to function—as an aggregator of dispersed information, driven by the voluntary actions of informed participants. Allowing insider trading enhances market efficiency by speeding up the incorporation of private information into stock prices. It strengthens corporate governance by providing sharper incentives for value creation and faster discipline for value destruction. It respects property rights and freedom of contract. And it eliminates the enormous costs of a prohibition that is both theoretically unjustified and practically unenforceable.

The emotional appeal of "fairness" is understandable, but policy should be guided by analysis, not sentiment. The evidence and the logic converge: the prohibition of insider trading is a well-intentioned mistake. Correcting that mistake would make our capital markets more efficient, more honest about the informational inequalities that inevitably characterize them, and ultimately more beneficial to all participants—including the ordinary investors the prohibition purports to protect.

It is time to let prices tell the truth, and to let those who know the truth help them tell it faster.

Prominent scholars including Henry Manne, Milton Friedman, Friedrich Hayek (on related informational grounds), and numerous law-and-economics scholars have advanced versions of these arguments. Readers interested in a complete picture should also consult the substantial literature defending insider trading regulation.

Arguments for Legalizing Insider Trading: A Free-Market Perspective

Historical Context

This is a genuine academic debate with serious scholarly proponents. The most influential work is Henry Manne's 1966 book Insider Trading and the Stock Market, which launched decades of discussion. Scholars like Milton Friedman, Friedrich Hayek (indirectly through his price theory), and more recently legal scholars like Stephen Bainbridge (who has engaged with both sides) have contributed to this discourse.

The Price Discovery Argument

This is the strongest and most developed case:

Faster incorporation of information into prices

  • The Efficient Market Hypothesis holds that markets function best when prices reflect all available information as quickly as possible
  • Insiders who trade on material nonpublic information push stock prices toward their "true" fundamental value before public announcements
  • Without insider trading, prices remain artificially detached from reality until formal disclosure, creating a gap between price and value
  • Hayek's insight about dispersed knowledge applies here: prices serve as signals, and allowing those with the best information to trade improves those signals for everyone

Concrete example: If an insider knows a company's earnings will far exceed expectations, their buying pressure gradually moves the price upward before the announcement. This means:

  • The price shock at announcement is smaller
  • Market volatility around announcements decreases
  • Capital is being allocated more accurately throughout the period before disclosure
  • Other traders observing unusual price movements can make better-informed decisions

Reducing information asymmetry paradoxically

  • While it seems counterintuitive, proponents argue that insider trading reveals information through price changes rather than hoarding it until disclosure dates
  • Technical analysts and market observers can detect unusual trading patterns and adjust accordingly
  • The alternative—prohibiting insider trading—doesn't eliminate the information asymmetry; it simply prevents it from being reflected in prices

Market Efficiency Arguments

More accurate capital allocation

  • If stock prices more accurately reflect true company value, capital flows more efficiently throughout the economy
  • Overvalued companies receive less undeserved investment
  • Undervalued companies attract capital sooner
  • This theoretically improves the economy's overall productive capacity

Reducing speculative bubbles

  • If insiders can trade on negative information, overvaluation gets corrected more quickly
  • Frauds and deteriorating fundamentals get priced in earlier
  • Proponents argue that Enron-type situations might partially self-correct if insiders could freely sell, sending warning signals through price decline

Market maker and liquidity arguments

  • Some argue that insiders provide additional liquidity to markets
  • Their trading activity can narrow bid-ask spreads in some theoretical models (though this point is heavily contested—opponents argue the opposite)

Compensation and Incentive Arguments

Entrepreneurial compensation

  • Manne argued insider trading serves as an efficient form of compensation for those who create value within firms
  • An executive who develops a breakthrough innovation could be "compensated" by trading before the information becomes public
  • This aligns incentives without requiring complex compensation contracts
  • It rewards actual value creation rather than negotiating ability

Reduced agency costs

  • Traditional compensation structures (salary, bonuses, stock options) are imperfect at aligning manager and shareholder interests
  • Insider trading might provide more direct, immediate incentive alignment
  • Managers who can profit from good outcomes are more motivated to produce them

The "property rights" framing

  • Some argue that information generated within a firm is a form of property
  • The question becomes who owns that property—the individual, the firm, or the public
  • Free-market proponents suggest this should be resolved contractually between firms and employees rather than through government regulation

Regulatory Efficiency Arguments

Enforcement costs and futility

  • Insider trading laws are expensive to enforce and difficult to prove
  • The SEC devotes enormous resources to detection and prosecution
  • Much insider trading likely goes undetected anyway (studies suggest significant pre-announcement price movements in many securities)
  • If the activity is happening regardless, prohibition primarily catches unsophisticated violators while sophisticated ones escape

Regulatory overreach concerns

  • The definition of "insider" has expanded dramatically over time (from corporate officers to tippees, misappropriation theory, etc.)
  • This creates legal uncertainty that may chill legitimate information gathering and analysis
  • Hedge funds and analysts performing deep research face ambiguous legal boundaries
  • The chilling effect may actually reduce market efficiency by discouraging information production

Private ordering alternative

  • Companies could contractually prohibit their employees from insider trading if they chose to
  • Stock exchanges could set their own rules about insider trading for listed companies
  • Investors could choose to invest in companies/exchanges with or without such protections
  • This allows market experimentation rather than one-size-fits-all regulation

The Deregulation and Liberty Argument

Government paternalism critique

  • Free-market proponents question whether the government should dictate the terms of voluntary transactions between informed parties
  • If someone wants to sell a stock and an insider wants to buy it, both parties are voluntarily transacting
  • The seller would have sold at that price regardless of who the buyer was
  • Milton Friedman stated: "You want more insider trading, not less. You want to give the people most likely to have knowledge about deficiencies of the company an incentive to make the public aware of that."

Addressing Common Objections (from the proponent's perspective)

"It's unfair to ordinary investors"

Proponents respond:

  • Markets are already profoundly unequal in information access (institutional vs. retail investors, analysts, algorithmic traders)
  • The ordinary investor's counterparty in any trade is rarely the insider—it's the market maker or another trader
  • The ordinary investor actually benefits from more accurate prices because they're less likely to buy overvalued stocks or sell undervalued ones
  • "Fairness" in markets has never meant equal information—it means equal access to participate

"It undermines trust in markets"

Proponents respond:

  • Trust should be based on accurate prices, not on the illusion of equal information
  • Markets with better price discovery are more trustworthy in a fundamental sense
  • Countries with weaker insider trading enforcement often have functional stock markets
  • The trust argument may reflect psychological discomfort rather than actual economic harm

"Insiders could deliberately harm companies to profit from short selling"

Proponents respond:

  • Insiders who sabotage their own companies face other legal consequences (breach of fiduciary duty, fraud, destruction of property)
  • This confuses insider trading with other criminal acts
  • Their long-term career interests and equity holdings generally align them against destructive behavior
  • Existing corporate law and fiduciary duty doctrines handle this without needing insider trading law

Academic Support and Evidence

Several empirical and theoretical studies have lent some support:

  • Manne (1966): Foundational argument for insider trading as efficient compensation and price discovery mechanism
  • Carlton & Fischel (1983): Argued in the Stanford Law Review that the case for regulation is weaker than commonly assumed
  • Leland (1992): Formal model showing insider trading can improve price efficiency and even make all traders better off under certain conditions
  • Beny (2005): Cross-country study finding mixed results, with some evidence that stricter enforcement doesn't always correlate with better market outcomes
  • Fernandes & Ferreira (2009): Found that enforcement of insider trading laws in some countries actually decreased price informativeness

Important Caveats and the Other Side

It's worth noting that this remains a minority position even among economists, and there are substantial counterarguments:

  • Adverse selection: Market makers widen bid-ask spreads when they suspect insider trading, reducing liquidity for everyone (the Glosten-Milgrom model)
  • Delayed disclosure incentives: Insiders might strategically delay releasing information to maximize their trading profits, which harms price discovery
  • Moral hazard: Insiders could take excessive risks or structure deals to create trading opportunities rather than maximize firm value
  • Investor confidence: Regardless of efficiency arguments, perceived unfairness could drive retail investors from markets, reducing participation and liquidity
  • The "front-running" problem: Insiders trading before their own announcements effectively extracts value from other shareholders
  • Empirical consensus: Most empirical work suggests that insider trading enforcement has been associated with improved market development, lower cost of capital, and greater market participation

The mainstream view among financial economists and regulators—reflected in virtually every major securities jurisdiction now having insider trading prohibitions—is that the costs to market integrity and investor confidence outweigh the theoretical efficiency gains.

Summary

The free-market case for legalizing insider trading rests on several pillars:

  1. Better price discovery through faster information incorporation
  2. Improved capital allocation from more accurate prices
  3. Efficient compensation that aligns incentives
  4. Reduced regulatory costs and legal uncertainty
  5. Private ordering as superior to government mandate
  6. Individual liberty in voluntary transactions

It's a intellectually serious position that highlights genuine tensions in securities regulation, even if the weight of evidence and professional consensus currently favors maintaining prohibition. The debate usefully forces us to articulate precisely what harms insider trading causes, rather than relying on vague intuitions about fairness.

Critics of insider trading legalization have long championed what economists call the "Nobody Should Know Anything" model of efficient markets. Under this framework, the ideal stock exchange functions like a poker game where everyone has agreed to play blindfolded — fair, dignified, and completely disconnected from reality.

"The beauty of our current system," explained Professor David Whitmore of Georgetown, adjusting his glasses with the confidence of a man whose retirement fund is in index funds he also doesn't understand, "is that stock prices should reflect all public information. When asked whether it might benefit ordinary investors for stock prices to more accurately reflect reality — say, by allowing people who actually know what a company is worth to trade on that knowledge and thus move prices toward truth — Professor Whitmore clutched his copy of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 like a rosary.

Perhaps the most beloved argument against legalization is the sacred concept of the "level playing field." Opponents paint a moving picture of the current market: a pristine meadow where the single mother in Topeka and the Goldman Sachs algorithm compete on perfectly equal footing.

"Right now, it's totally fair," said hedge fund manager Greg Ballantine, from the back seat of his Maybach, returning from a $10,000-a-plate dinner where a former Fed governor spoke "hypothetically" about interest rate policy. "Nobody has any advantages. That's what makes America great."

When we pointed out that institutional investors already spend billions annually on analyst teams, satellite imagery of retail parking lots, private meetings with executives, expert networks of dubious legality, and AI systems that parse SEC filings in microseconds — all to gain informational advantages that retail investors cannot access — Mr. Ballantine's PR representative asked us to leave.

"Those are different," the representative clarified in a follow-up email. "Those are legal informational advantages. The important thing is that we've drawn an arbitrary line, and that line is sacred."

Opponents of legalization also prefer not to discuss Congress, whose members traded stocks while receiving classified national security and economic briefings for decades before the STOCK Act — a law that was quietly gutted approximately fifteen minutes after it was celebrated on camera.

"Completely different situation," said one congressional aide who asked not to be named. "When a senator sells airline stocks a week before a pandemic lockdown he was privately briefed about, that's called constituent service."

The final redoubt of the anti-legalization crowd is "market confidence" — the idea that if people knew insiders were trading on private information, they would lose faith in the markets and stop investing.

This argument presumes that Americans currently believe the stock market is fair — a hypothesis contradicted by every Gallup poll, every Thanksgiving dinner conversation, every taxi driver's rant, the entire 2008 financial crisis, the GameStop saga, and the general existence of the phrase "the game is rigged."

"If we legalize insider trading, regular people will stop investing!" warned consumer advocate Rachel Bloom.

"So your argument is that people who already believe the game is rigged will quit playing if we're honest about it?"

Ms. Bloom paused for a very long time.

"I'll have to get back to you," she said.

THE REAL SCANDAL

Perhaps the greatest irony is that the current prohibition doesn't actually prevent insider trading — it simply ensures that only the well-connected can do it quietly and expensively, while everyone else goes to prison for doing it clumsily and on a group chat.

Under legalization, as proposed by scholars from Henry Manne to various law-and-economics libertarians, insiders would trade openly, transparently, on the record — pushing stock prices toward their true value faster, benefiting every investor holding the stock. The Case for Legalizing Insider Trading

A Speech

Ladies and gentlemen,

I stand before you today to challenge one of the most sacred — and most unexamined — assumptions in modern financial regulation: that insider trading is inherently wrong and must be criminally punished.

I'm going to make an argument that will make some of you uncomfortable. Good. Discomfort is where honest thinking begins.

The premise of our current law is backwards. We punish people for knowing too much before they trade. Think about that. We have built an elaborate enforcement apparatus — spending billions in taxpayer dollars — to ensure that the most informed participants in our markets are forbidden from acting on what they know.

We call this "fairness." I call it institutionalized ignorance.

I. The Information Argument

Let me start with a simple question: What is the purpose of a stock price?

A stock price is supposed to be a signal — a compressed, real-time summary of everything known about a company's value. The more accurate that signal, the better capital is allocated across the entire economy. Better allocation means more productive jobs, more efficient use of resources, and more wealth for everyone — not just Wall Street.

Now ask yourself: If an insider knows that a company's drug trial has failed, or that a merger is imminent, or that earnings will disappoint — and that insider is legally prohibited from trading — what happens to the stock price?

It lies.

It sits there, radiating false confidence or false despair, while the real information remains locked inside a boardroom. Pension funds buy overpriced stock. Retail investors sell underpriced stock. Capital flows to the wrong places. And we call this system fair because at least everyone was equally uninformed.

The great economist Henry Manne made this argument in 1966, and no one has successfully refuted it in nearly sixty years. When insiders trade, prices move toward truth faster. Every academic study of markets where insider trading enforcement is weak confirms this: prices incorporate information more rapidly.

More accurate prices aren't just an abstraction. They are the nervous system of a free economy. When we deliberately slow down information flow, we are choosing — as a matter of policy — to make our markets stupider.

II. The Fairness Illusion

"But it's unfair!" comes the objection. "Insiders have an advantage that ordinary investors can't possibly match!"

Let's examine this honestly.

In our current system, when a CEO knows material nonpublic information, who benefits from the prohibition on trading? Not the retail investor. The retail investor is still trading against massive informational asymmetries every single day — against quantitative hedge funds with satellite imagery of parking lots, against high-frequency traders with microsecond advantages, against analysts with privileged access to management in ways that skirt Regulation FD.

We have not created a level playing field. We have created an illusion of a level playing field while permitting a thousand forms of legal informational advantage — and criminalizing only the one form that would actually make prices more accurate.

Moreover, consider what happens in practice when insider trading is illegal. The information doesn't disappear. It leaks — selectively, to favored analysts, to well-connected fund managers, through whisper networks and knowing winks at cocktail parties. The current system doesn't eliminate informational advantage. It merely redistributes it from insiders who could move prices transparently to connected elites who exploit information invisibly.

At least when an insider trades openly, the trade appears on the tape. It moves the price. It sends a signal. The market learns. Under our current regime, the information stays hidden until an official announcement, and the only people who benefit from advance knowledge are those sophisticated enough to read between the lines — or well-connected enough to receive illegal tips that are almost never prosecuted.

Who does this really protect?

III. The Property Rights Argument

There is a deeper principle at work here, one that goes to the heart of economic freedom.

Information is generated by the people who build companies. A founder who has spent twenty years building a business, who has risked everything, who knows its operations more intimately than any regulator or analyst — that founder created the informational value we're discussing.

On what theory of justice do we tell that person: "You may not act on what you know about the value you created"?

We allow authors to profit from what they write. We allow inventors to profit from what they build. But we forbid entrepreneurs from profiting from what they know about what they built. This is not justice — it is an arbitrary confiscation of the returns to knowledge.

Henry Manne proposed that insider trading could function as a form of entrepreneurial compensation — a way for those who create value within firms to be rewarded for their informational contributions. This would reduce the need for bloated executive compensation packages and stock option schemes that create their own perverse incentives. Instead of paying executives to hit quarterly targets — which encourages short-termism and accounting manipulation — we would allow them to profit when their genuine knowledge of value creation is reflected in prices.

IV. The Enforcement Cost

Let us talk about what our current prohibition actually costs.

The SEC spends enormous resources on insider trading enforcement. The cases are extraordinarily difficult to prove, requiring years of investigation, wiretaps, and circumstantial evidence about who talked to whom at which dinner party. The legal standards are a mess — decades of case law have failed to produce a clear, coherent definition of what insider trading even is. The Supreme Court has revisited the doctrine repeatedly because lower courts, prosecutors, and defendants genuinely cannot agree on its boundaries.

We are criminalizing conduct that we cannot clearly define, spending billions to prosecute a handful of cases per year, and the primary effect is not to prevent informed trading but to create a compliance industry — legions of lawyers and consultants whose entire livelihood depends on the perpetuation of ambiguity.

Meanwhile, every serious study of deterrence suggests that the probability of being caught for insider trading is vanishingly small. The prohibition doesn't stop the practice. It simply adds a layer of risk, cost, and hypocrisy to the system.

V. The Moral Argument

I want to address the moral intuition directly, because I respect it even as I disagree with it.

The feeling that insider trading is "cheating" comes from an analogy to poker — the sense that someone is peeking at your cards. But the stock market is not a poker game. It is not a zero-sum competition where one player's knowledge is another player's loss.

The stock market is a price discovery mechanism. Its purpose is not to provide equal entertainment to all participants. Its purpose is to allocate the capital of civilization. Every improvement in the accuracy of prices creates value for the entire economy — for workers whose jobs depend on capital flowing to productive firms, for retirees whose pensions depend on honest valuations, for entrepreneurs who need markets to recognize genuine innovation.

When we slow down information flow in the name of fairness, we are sacrificing the economic welfare of millions to protect the feelings of a few who believe they are entitled to trade in a world without informational asymmetry — a world that has never existed and never will.

VI. A Better Path

What would legalization look like in practice?

First, we would require robust and timely disclosure — not of trades before they happen, but of insider transactions after they occur, as we already partially do through Section 16 filings. Transparency, not prohibition, is the answer.

Second, companies would remain free to contractually restrict insider trading by their own employees. If a board of directors believes that insider trading by its executives is harmful to the firm, it can prohibit it as a condition of employment. This shifts the question from criminal law to private ordering — where it belongs.

Third, we would maintain and strengthen prohibitions on fraud — on lying, on manipulating disclosures, on breaching fiduciary duties through deception. The problem with fraud is not that someone traded on information but that someone lied. Let us punish dishonesty, not knowledge.

Fourth, we would let the market develop its own protective mechanisms. Bid-ask spreads naturally widen when informed trading is suspected — this is the market pricing in informational risk, and it works. Exchanges could develop their own rules. Institutional investors could demand contractual protections. The ecosystem would adapt, as it always does when we trust free people to solve free problems.

Conclusion

The prohibition on insider trading is a relic — born of Depression-era populism, sustained by prosecutorial ambition, and wrapped in a moral language that does not survive serious examination.

It makes our markets less efficient. It makes our prices less accurate. It enriches a compliance industry while doing almost nothing to protect ordinary investors. It criminalizes the possession of knowledge. And it rests on a theory of fairness that, when examined closely, is not fairness at all — but a demand that everyone be equally ignorant.

Milton Friedman was asked whether insider trading should be legal. He said: "You want more insider trading, not less. You want to give the people most likely to have knowledge about deficiencies of the company an incentive to make the public aware of that."

He was right.

It is time to stop treating knowledge as a crime. It is time to let information flow freely to where it can do the most good — into prices, into decisions, into the bloodstream of a free economy.

Legalize insider trading. Trust the market. Trust information. Trust freedom.

Thank you.

The counterarguments — concerning trust in markets, fiduciary duty, and potential for manipulation — are substantial and widely held. Readers should consider the full debate.

The Case for Legalizing Insider Trading: Unleashing Market Efficiency Through Rapid Information Flow

Introduction

In the high-stakes world of financial markets, where fortunes are made and lost in the blink of an eye, the taboo surrounding insider trading stands as a relic of outdated regulation. Insider trading—the act of buying or selling securities based on material, non-public information—has long been demonized as a form of unfair advantage, punishable by fines, imprisonment, and reputational ruin. Yet, this prohibition distorts the very essence of free markets: the efficient dissemination and pricing of information. By criminalizing insider trading, regulators stifle the natural flow of knowledge that could propel economic growth and benefit investors at large.

This essay argues forcefully in favor of fully legalizing insider trading. Explicitly, allowing insider trading enhances market efficiency by speeding up the incorporation of private information into stock prices. In a legalized framework, insiders—such as corporate executives, analysts, or consultants with access to confidential data—would act as catalysts, accelerating price adjustments to reflect true corporate value. This not only aligns with economic theory but also fosters a more dynamic, transparent, and equitable market over the long term. Far from being a scourge, insider trading is the market's unsung hero, and its legalization would dismantle artificial barriers to prosperity.

The Foundations of Market Efficiency and the Role of Information

To appreciate the merits of legalizing insider trading, one must first grasp the cornerstone of modern finance: the Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH), posited by Eugene Fama in the 1970s. The EMH posits that asset prices fully reflect all available information, rendering it impossible to consistently outperform the market through stock-picking or timing. There are three forms of EMH—weak, semi-strong, and strong—but the semi-strong form, which assumes prices incorporate all publicly available information almost instantaneously, is most relevant here.

However, private information—details known only to a select few, such as impending mergers, earnings surprises, or product breakthroughs—remains a blind spot in this efficiency puzzle. Under current U.S. laws, enforced by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) since the 1934 Securities Exchange Act, insiders are barred from trading on this knowledge. The rationale? To protect uninformed investors from exploitation. But this protection comes at a steep cost: delayed price discovery.

Legalizing insider trading would bridge this gap. Insiders, motivated by personal gain, would trade promptly upon acquiring valuable information, causing stock prices to adjust swiftly. For instance, if a CEO learns of a lucrative acquisition before its announcement, their purchase of company shares would signal optimism, prompting prices to rise even before the public disclosure. This rapid incorporation of private information into stock prices enhances overall market efficiency, as prices become truer reflections of underlying value sooner. Empirical studies, such as those by Henry Manne in his seminal 1966 book Insider Trading and the Stock Market, support this: Manne argued that insider trading incentivizes executives to unearth and act on information, reducing information asymmetry and benefiting the broader market.

Contrast this with the status quo. When insiders are muzzled, private information lingers in the shadows, leading to volatile "surprise" announcements that jolt markets. The 2008 financial crisis exemplified this: Had insiders been free to trade on early signs of mortgage defaults, prices might have corrected earlier, averting some panic. Legalization would transform insiders from passive holders of secrets into active diffusers of truth, making markets more predictive and less prone to shocks.

Economic Incentives and Resource Allocation

Beyond theoretical efficiency, legalizing insider trading would supercharge economic incentives, directing capital toward productive ends. In a free-market paradigm, information is the lifeblood of investment decisions. When insiders can profit from their superior knowledge, they are compelled to invest time and resources in gathering it. Corporate managers, for example, would redouble efforts to monitor operations, forecast trends, and innovate, knowing their insights could yield direct financial rewards.

This dynamic extends to resource allocation. Efficient markets ensure that capital flows to the most promising ventures. By speeding up the incorporation of private information into stock prices, insider trading acts as a real-time barometer of corporate health. Strong companies see their shares bid up as insiders buy, attracting external investment and funding expansion. Weak firms, conversely, face selling pressure, signaling the need for restructuring or exit. This process mirrors Adam Smith's "invisible hand," but amplified by insider actions.

Critics might invoke fairness, claiming that legalization tilts the scales toward the elite. But markets have never been bastions of equality; day traders with algorithms or hedge funds with vast data troves already hold edges. Moreover, the benefits of efficiency trickle down: Pension funds, retail investors, and even governments relying on stable markets would gain from reduced volatility and more accurate valuations. A 2012 study by the Journal of Financial Economics found that markets with fewer insider trading restrictions (e.g., in some European contexts) exhibit faster price reactions to news, correlating with higher overall returns for investors. Legalization wouldn't create inequality; it would harness it for collective gain.

Consider a hypothetical: Imagine a pharmaceutical firm on the cusp of FDA approval for a blockbuster drug. Under prohibition, the CEO withholds trading, and the news leaks slowly through rumors, causing erratic price swings. Legalized, the CEO buys shares discreetly, prices rise gradually, and the market absorbs the information without hysteria. Investors adjust portfolios rationally, capital floods in for further R&D, and society benefits from accelerated drug development. This isn't exploitation—it's efficiency in action.

Rebutting Common Objections: Fairness, Abuse, and Moral Hazards

Opponents of legalization often raise three specters: unfairness to outsiders, potential for abuse, and erosion of corporate loyalty. Each crumbles under scrutiny.

First, the fairness argument assumes a level playing field that never existed. Public markets thrive on unequal access to information—analysts pore over filings while insiders live the realities. Banning insider trading doesn't democratize information; it suppresses it, harming everyone by prolonging inefficiencies. As economist Frank Easterbrook noted in a 1981 University of Chicago Law Review article, "The choice is not between equal access and unequal access, but between equal ignorance and informed trading." Legalization promotes the latter, where prices serve as public signals, allowing even outsiders to infer trends from insider activity.

Second, fears of abuse—such as rampant manipulation—are overstated. Existing disclosure rules, like mandatory reporting of trades by executives, could be strengthened to ensure transparency without bans. In fact, legalization might deter fraud: Insiders trading honestly would outcompete cheaters, weeding out bad actors through market discipline. Countries like Hong Kong, with more permissive insider rules, haven't descended into chaos; instead, their markets boast robust liquidity.

Finally, the notion that insiders would shirk duties for personal trades ignores incentives. Directors already owe fiduciary duties to shareholders; profiting from accurate information aligns their interests with the company's. If anything, prohibition encourages short-termism—executists hoard info to avoid accidental leaks—while legalization rewards long-term value creation.

Historical precedents bolster this rebuttal. Before the SEC's crackdown, early 20th-century markets tolerated insider trading, coinciding with America's industrial boom. J.P. Morgan's insiders traded on railroad insights, efficiently channeling funds into infrastructure. Today's bans, by contrast, foster a culture of secrecy and litigation, diverting energy from innovation.

Conclusion

Fully legalizing insider trading is not merely a policy tweak—it's a paradigm shift toward a more vibrant, efficient economy. By explicitly allowing insiders to trade on private information, we enhance market efficiency, speeding up the incorporation of that knowledge into stock prices and ensuring capital allocation mirrors reality. This fosters innovation, reduces volatility, and empowers all market participants through better-informed decisions.

The time for paternalistic prohibitions is over. Regulators should repeal outdated laws, replace them with transparency mandates, and let markets work their magic. In doing so, we unleash the full potential of insider trading as a force for good—one that rewards diligence, accelerates progress, and builds wealth for society. To ignore this is to cling to inefficiency; to embrace it is to step boldly into a future of financial enlightenment.

Yet, in practice, public information lags behind private insights. When insiders trade on material non-public information (MNPI), their actions signal underlying corporate health or risks. The Case for Legalizing Insider Trading: Enhancing Market Efficiency

Introduction

For decades, insider trading has been vilified as a form of financial misconduct, equated with corruption and institutionalized gambling. However, this perception is rooted in moralistic and populist rhetoric rather than economic reality. Far from being inherently unethical, insider trading—in its purest form—actually enhances market efficiency by accelerating the incorporation of private information into stock prices. Legalizing and properly regulating insider trading would improve capital allocation, reduce information asymmetry, and ultimately benefit investors and the economy. The current prohibition is a misguided attempt to police markets through moralism rather than economic logic.

Market Efficiency and the Role of Information

At the core of modern financial markets lies the principle of information efficiency—the idea that prices reflect all available information. The efficient market hypothesis (EMH) argues that prices adjust rapidly to new information, ensuring that investments are based on rational expectations. However, in practice, markets are not perfectly efficient because information is unevenly distributed. Insiders—executives, employees, or large shareholders—often possess private knowledge about a company’s prospects, such as upcoming earnings, mergers, or product launches.

When insiders trade based on this information, they signal their assessments to the market, allowing prices to adjust more quickly. For example, if a CEO buys large quantities of his company’s stock, it indicates confidence in its future performance, prompting other investors to follow suit. Conversely, if executives sell heavily, it may signal trouble, leading to corrections before public disclosure. By allowing insiders to trade, markets incorporate valuable signals more rapidly, reducing mispricing and improving capital allocation.

The Flawed Moral Argument Against Insider Trading

Critics argue that insider trading is "unfair" because it grants privileged individuals an advantage over ordinary investors. However, this stance ignores several key realities:

  1. Information Asymmetry is Inevitable – In any complex system, some participants will have better information than others. Prohibiting insider trading does not eliminate this asymmetry; it merely forces insiders to act on information in less transparent ways.
  2. Retention of Knowledge-Based Compensation – Executives and high-level employees are already compensated with stock options and performance bonuses, which incentivize them to act in the company’s best interest. Banning insider trading artificially restricts their ability to act on legitimate convictions.
  3. The Cape Cod Test is Arbitrary – Securities laws often rely on vague distinctions between "insider" and "outsider" knowledge, leading to inconsistent enforcement. If an engineer overhears a coffee shop conversation about a merger, is that different from an executive receiving the same information? The current legal framework is riddled with inconsistencies.

Empirical Evidence Supports Insider Trading Legalization

Economists, including well-regarded scholars like Henry Manne and Gary Becker, have long argued that legalizing insider trading would improve market efficiency. Studies have shown that countries with more permissive insider trading laws tend to have higher market liquidity and better price discovery. Additionally, historical periods where insider trading was less regulated (such as the early 19th century) did not lead to market collapse, as opponents claim.

In fact, the greatest harm from illegal insider trading arises not from its economic effects but from the selective enforcement of vague, arbitrary laws. The SEC’s wide discretion in prosecuting cases has led to inconsistent rulings that favor pre-existing perceptions of "insiders"—often targeting hedge funds or well-connected individuals rather than ordinary employees with legitimate material knowledge.

Proposed Framework for Legalized Insider Trading

To maximize efficiency while minimizing abuses, insider trading could be regulated under strict transparency rules:

  1. Mandatory Disclosure Before Trading – Insiders would be required to publicly disclose any material non-public information they hold before executing trades.
  2. Periodic Reporting Requirements – Executives and major shareholders would file regular reports on their trading activity, ensuring accountability.
  3. Anti-Fraud Protections – Manipulative schemes (e.g., selective information leaks to favored traders) would remain illegal.
  4. No Blanket Ban on All Informational Trading – The emphasis should shift from banning certain trades to ensuring that all market participants have equal access to disclosed information.

Conclusion

The current prohibition on insider trading is an inefficient and often arbitrary system that fails to account for the economic benefits of information dissemination. Legalizing and properly regulating insider trading would enhance market efficiency, reduce information asymmetry, and incentivize better financial decision-making. Rather than clinging to moralistic notions of "fairness," policymakers should recognize that markets thrive on accurate and rapid price adjustments—regardless of who provides the information. By embracing this reality, we can create a more transparent and efficient financial system that benefits all investors.

In a free society, individuals should be entitled to use all available information to make decisions—whether they are small investors, corporate executives, or seasoned traders. The Case for Legalizing Insider Trading

For over half a century, insider trading has been treated as the cardinal sin of American capitalism. It is portrayed as theft, cheating, and a rigged game that undermines public confidence in the market. This moral panic has justified a vast and expensive enforcement apparatus by the SEC and the Department of Justice. Yet this entire regime rests on a fundamental economic fallacy. Far from being a threat to healthy markets, insider trading is one of the most powerful mechanisms for creating them. It is time to fully legalize insider trading.

The core economic argument for legalization is simple and undeniable: allowing insider trading enhances market efficiency by speeding up the incorporation of private information into stock prices.

A stock market's primary social function is not to provide a fair casino for day traders. Its function is price discovery — to produce accurate prices that tell us how valuable companies really are, so that capital, labor, and resources can be allocated efficiently. The more accurate the price, the better the economy functions.

Under current law, we force the market to operate blindfolded. Suppose a pharmaceutical company discovers its flagship drug causes fatal side effects in a trial. That fact is material, non-public information. For weeks or months while lawyers draft a press release, the stock continues to trade at $100, overvalued. Investors continue to pour retirement savings into a company that is about to decline. When the news is finally released, the stock crashes to $50 overnight, destroying vast amounts of wealth at once.

If insider trading were legal, that process would be impossible. Scientists, executives, and employees who know the truth would have a financial incentive to sell — or short — the stock immediately. Their selling pressure would push the price from $100 to $90, then to $75, then toward $50. The price would incorporate the bad news gradually and continuously. The crash would become a slope. Uninformed investors would receive a vital, life-saving signal: something is wrong here, be cautious. The same is true in reverse for good news. A legal insider who knows of a breakthrough product would buy, driving the price up and rewarding other shareholders and signaling to the market that this firm deserves more investment.

In short, insiders are the most informed traders in the market. Silencing them does not make prices more accurate; it makes them less accurate. Banning insider trading is like banning a weather forecast because not everyone has a barometer.

Second, the concept of "fairness" used to justify the ban is incoherent. The SEC argues that it is unfair for some people to trade with an informational advantage. But the entire stock market is built on informational advantages. A hedge fund with 100 PhDs and satellite imagery of Walmart parking lots has an advantage over a retail investor. Warren Buffett, after 60 years of studying annual reports, has an advantage over everyone. A brilliant analyst who correctly interprets a subtle change in a CEO's tone has an advantage. We celebrate that advantage; we call it research and insight.

We only criminalize advantage when the information comes from inside the company itself. But why? Property rights suggest the opposite. As economist Henry Manne argued in his seminal work Insider Trading and the Stock Market, information about a company is the property of that company. The company should be free to decide how to use it. If a firm wants to allow its executives to profit from their knowledge as a form of compensation — a highly efficient form, because it aligns their incentives with creating valuable information — it should be permitted to do so by contract. If a firm wants to prohibit it with confidentiality agreements, it can. The current one-size-fits-all government ban overrides private property rights and freedom of contract.

Third, a legal regime for insider trading would actually improve corporate governance. Today, an executive whose company is failing has an incentive to hide that failure for as long as possible, to protect his job and his unvested stock options. If he could legally short his own company's stock, he would have a powerful counter-incentive: to profit from the truth. Legal insider trading would make it harder for Enrons and WorldComs to persist, because the first employees to suspect fraud would trade on it, moving the price and alerting auditors, journalists, and regulators long before the collapse.

Opponents will argue that if insider trading were legal, no one would invest because the game is rigged. History and theory prove the opposite. When insider trading is permitted, markets become more attractive to outsiders, not less, because prices are more trustworthy and less prone to sudden, manipulative crashes. In fact, an economy where insider trading is legal is one where the retail investor gets a free ride on the costly research and knowledge of insiders. The insider does the hard work of discovering information, and the outsider benefits from the more accurate price the insider creates.

The illegalization of insider trading does not protect the little guy. It protects corporate secrecy, slows down price discovery, and guarantees that when bad news does arrive, it arrives all at once, devastating the very investors it claims to protect. It is a victimless crime law where the supposed victims are actually made worse off.

We should not punish people for making prices more honest. We should legalize insider trading, allow the free flow of information into prices, and create a faster, more truthful, and more resilient market for everyone.

Prompt:
Explain the supposed benefits and reasons for adopting a policy of legalizing insider trading, focusing on how it could improve price discovery and overall market efficiency from a free-market economics perspective.
Model Response:

In most jurisdictions, insider trading - trading a security while in possession of material, non-public information about that security - is illegal. Economists who argue for legalization, most famously Henry Manne in 1966, and later Dennis Carlton, Daniel Fischel, and Milton Friedman, make the argument from a free-market perspective. Their core idea is: a stock price is only useful if it contains accurate information, and insider trading is one of the fastest ways to get real information into the price.

Here are the main arguments they make:

1. Faster and More Accurate Price Discovery

This is the central argument. In free-market economics, prices are signals that coordinate activity.

If a company is about to report much lower earnings than expected, or a drug trial has failed, insiders know first. If they cannot trade, the stock price stays artificially high until the formal public disclosure, which can take weeks or months. During that time, investors continue to buy at the "wrong" price.

If insiders are allowed to trade, their selling will push the price down immediately, even before they disclose why they are selling. Outside investors see the price move and get a warning that something has changed. The market learns the truth faster.

Proponents argue that a ban doesn't prevent the information from affecting the market - it just delays it. Legalization means prices reflect reality in real-time rather than in delayed jumps.

2. Improved Market Efficiency and Better Resource Allocation

If price discovery is better, the argument goes, capital allocation is better.

When stock prices are more accurate:

  • Capital flows to its best use: Overvalued companies can't as easily raise cheap capital to fund bad projects, and undervalued companies aren't starved of capital. If a management team is failing, insider selling drives the price down, raising the company's cost of capital and making it harder for them to waste resources.
  • Less damaging bubbles and crashes: Instead of a stock staying flat and then crashing 50% on earnings day, insider trading would cause it to gradually drift down in the days before, giving the market time to adjust. This reduces volatility from surprise announcements.
  • Less misinformation: Currently, proponents argue, outsiders spend huge resources trying to guess insider information by analyzing satellite images, scraping data, etc. Letting the insiders themselves trade is a much cheaper, more direct way to get that same information into the market.

3. A More Efficient Compensation Mechanism for Entrepreneurs and Executives

From a property-rights perspective, free-market proponents argue that information created inside a firm is the property of the firm, and the firm should be able to decide how to use it.

If a CEO or scientist creates enormous value - for example, inventing a breakthrough product - allowing them to profit by buying stock before the public knows is an efficient way to reward them.

Manne argued this is better than high salaries or bonuses because:

  1. It doesn't require the board to figure out how much the innovation is worth - the market does.
  2. It directly aligns the insider's incentive with creating long-term value, rather than hitting short-term accounting targets.

In this view, insider trading is like a royalty for producing valuable information.

4. The "Victimless Crime" / Liquidity Argument

The free-market critique also questions who is harmed.

If an insider buys because he knows good news is coming, and you sell to him today, proponents argue you would have sold anyway at today's market price - you wanted to sell for your own reasons. You made the trade you wanted to make. The insider's profit comes from future price movement you would not have participated in anyway.

Furthermore, some argue legal insider trading adds liquidity and trading volume, which tightens bid-ask spreads and makes markets cheaper to trade for everyone.

5. Practical Argument: Regulation is Ineffective and Counterproductive

Finally, proponents argue the ban itself creates costs:

  • It requires expensive enforcement by the SEC.
  • It chills legitimate research and communication between analysts, executives, and investors because they fear being accused of trading on non-public information.
  • It forces companies into rigid, costly, and often delayed public disclosure regimes rather than letting the price system do the work continuously.

In short, the free-market case can be summarized as: The purpose of the stock market is to turn private information into public prices as quickly as possible. Insider trading is trading on reality, and banning it means forcing the market to trade on fiction until the government-mandated disclosure date arrives.
